title: GPT-2: no fine-tuning, just a prompt, and the language model teaches itself tasks
summary: GPT-2 scales GPT-1 up to 1.5 billion parameters and 40 GB of web text, then drops fine-tuning entirely: write the task as a prompt and the model does reading comprehension, summarization, translation, and QA zero-shot. We unpack the core idea that a task is also text, WebText and byte-level BPE, how each task is prompted and scored, and how the paper checks for memorization — plus the parameter count it got wrong.
ai_summary: "Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners" (OpenAI, 2019) argues that a language model trained on large and diverse text learns many tasks without explicit supervision. The authors built 40 GB of WebText from Reddit links with karma, trained GPT-2 with up to 1.5 billion parameters, kept the GPT-1 structure but switched to pre-layer norm, byte-level BPE, and a 1,024-token context. With no fine-tuning and only a prompt, GPT-2 set zero-shot records on 7 of 8 language modeling datasets and scored 55 F1 on CoQA reading comprehension, but summarization, translation, and QA were still rudimentary. Everything improved with model size, and the largest model still underfits.
brief: Problem: every task requires its own labeled dataset, and multi-task learning doesn't scale. Can a model learn tasks from natural language itself?
Method: train a Transformer decoder with up to 1.5 billion parameters on 40 GB of WebText. With no fine-tuning, write each task as a prompt and let the model continue.
Results: new zero-shot records on 7 of 8 language modeling datasets; 55 F1 on CoQA; summarization, translation, and QA are still rudimentary but improve steadily with model size.
Limits: zero-shot is far from practical, and the paper's reported parameter counts are wrong. GPT-3 later makes this path work with few-shot prompting and much more scale.

paper.title: Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners
paper.authors: Alec Radford, Jeffrey Wu, Rewon Child, David Luan, Dario Amodei, Ilya Sutskever

cover.headline: A close read of the original GPT-2 paper

big.label: GPT-2 has over an order of magnitude more parameters than GPT-1.

sections.h: The bottom line: what this paper actually did

blocks.p: In February 2019, OpenAI's Alec Radford, Jeffrey Wu, Rewon Child, David Luan, Dario Amodei, and Ilya Sutskever released this paper. Like its predecessor GPT-1, it was not posted on arXiv but appeared as a PDF on OpenAI's website. The largest model in the paper, **GPT-2**, has 1.5 billion parameters — more than ten times as many as GPT-1.

Its core claim is right in the title: **language models are unsupervised multitask learners**. Train a model to guess the next word on enough large and varied text, and it will **learn many tasks on its own** — reading comprehension, summarization, translation, question answering — with no fine-tuning and no architecture changes. You just write the task as a piece of text and let the model continue. This is called **zero-shot**.

To test this, the authors crawled more than 8 million web pages from links that had been upvoted on Reddit, producing 40 GB of text called WebText. GPT-2 then set zero-shot records on 7 of 8 language modeling datasets; given a passage and the dialogue history, it scored 55 F1 on CoQA reading comprehension, matching or beating 3 of 4 supervised baselines that used over 127,000 human-labeled question-answer pairs. On summarization, translation, and QA, it was still far from practical, but every task improved steadily as the model grew.

This paper is the bridge in the main story: GPT-1 showed that pre-training + fine-tuning works, with a hint of zero-shot at the end; GPT-2 made that hint the main act, **turning "do tasks with a prompt and no fine-tuning" into a serious research direction**; a year later GPT-3 scaled up more than another 100x and made it genuinely useful with few-shot prompting.

callout.title: The one-sentence version
callout.text: GPT-2 = GPT-1's architecture with small changes + scaled to 1.5 billion parameters + trained on 40 GB of high-quality web text. With no fine-tuning, you write the task as a text prefix — for example, append "TL;DR:" to an article to get a summary — and the model can do reading comprehension, summarization, translation, and QA. Performance rises steadily with model size, and the largest model still underfits.

callout.title: Three concepts to know before reading
callout.text: Not knowing them is fine — these three are enough:
list: **GPT-1** — a Transformer decoder pre-trained on books and then fine-tuned for specific tasks. See the previous article in this series on GPT-1.
**Zero-shot** — the model sees no training examples for the task, updates no parameters, and does the task directly.
**Perplexity (PPL)** — a measure of how "surprised" a language model is by text. A perplexity of 10 roughly means the model is choosing among 10 words at each step; lower is better.

sections.h: Problem: a labeled dataset for every task doesn't scale

blocks.p: The paper opens bluntly: machine-learning systems of the time were "narrow experts" rather than "competent generalists." The standard recipe was to collect demonstrations for each task, train a model to imitate them, and evaluate on held-out data from the same distribution. These systems were brittle to small changes in data distribution or task specification.

Multi-task learning looked like a way out, but the authors do the math: from a meta-learning perspective, each (dataset, objective) pair is just one training example. The two most ambitious multi-task studies at the time used only 10 and 17 such pairs, while current methods usually need hundreds or thousands of examples to learn something that generalizes. Manually accumulating datasets and designing objectives was unlikely to scale far enough.
So the paper takes a different approach: **can a model learn tasks from natural language itself, without a human specifying which part is the input and which is the answer?**

sections.h: Core idea: the task itself can be written as text

blocks.p: The paper reframes "doing a task" in probabilistic terms: learning a task is estimating the conditional distribution p(output | input). But a general system may need to do different tasks with the same input, so it should estimate **p(output | input, task)** — conditioned not only on the input but also on the task.

Previously, "what to do" was communicated through model architecture (task-specific encoders and decoders) or training algorithms. The paper points out that **language itself can flexibly specify tasks, inputs, and outputs**. A translation example can be written as one sequence: (translate to French, English text, French text); a reading-comprehension example can be: (answer the question, document, question, answer).

parts.desc: A piece of text made up of tokens s_{1}, …, s_{n}.
The probability that the next token is s_{i} given all previous tokens. This is what a language model learns.
The probability of the whole text is the product of these step-by-step probabilities. This lets the model both score any text and generate it token by token.

formula.note: The key insight: if the task, input, and answer are all written in the same text, then predicting the answer is just part of predicting the next token. As the paper puts it, the supervised objective is the same as the unsupervised objective, only evaluated on a subset of the sequence. So the global minimum of the unsupervised objective is also the global minimum of the supervised objective.

plain.title: A task is just text too
plain.text: A language model does only one thing: guess the next word given the earlier text. GPT-2's idea is that task instructions, examples, and questions can all be written as the earlier text, and the answer is simply the most likely continuation. If the model reads enough, it can continue in the right way.

callout.title: The web is full of natural demonstrations
callout.text: The paper found many naturally occurring translation demonstrations in WebText, such as "as the French say: Je ne suis pas un imbecile (I'm not a fool)," or an English report that quotes a French sentence and then gives its English translation. A model trying to predict the next word accurately — if it is big enough — will learn along the way that after French text followed by something like "which means," an English translation should come next. The authors' guess: with enough capacity, language models will infer and perform tasks demonstrated in text simply to predict that text better.

blocks.p: The paper concedes this is only true in principle. The real question is whether the unsupervised objective can be optimized well enough in practice. Early experiments showed that large enough language models can indeed learn multiple tasks this way, just much more slowly than with explicit supervision.

sections.h: Data: WebText, filtered by humans first

blocks.p: To show the model as many task demonstrations as possible, the data must be **both large and diverse**. Earlier language models trained mostly on a single domain: news, Wikipedia, or fiction. Web crawls such as Common Crawl are far larger but much messier, with one study finding many documents "whose content is mostly unintelligible."

The authors' compromise: scrape only pages that **humans have already filtered**. They took every outbound link from Reddit with at least 3 karma (upvotes), treating it as a rough signal that someone found the link interesting, useful, or funny.

fig.title: WebText: 45 million links, cleaned down to 8 million+ documents and 40 GB
fig.subtitle: Compiled from section 2.1 of the paper
rows: All outbound links from Reddit with at least 3 karma — 45 million total
Use Dragnet and Newspaper to extract text from HTML
Deduplicate and apply heuristic cleaning, leaving over 8 million documents and 40 GB of text
All Wikipedia documents: many evaluation datasets also draw from Wikipedia, so removing them reduces training/test overlap

blocks.p: **Input representation** — to let the model score **any string**, GPT-2 switches to **byte-level BPE**. Ordinary BPE works on Unicode code points, so covering all Unicode symbols would require a base vocabulary of over 130,000; byte-level BPE needs only 256 bytes. But applying BPE directly to bytes would merge common words into many near-duplicate tokens like dog, dog., dog!, dog? and waste the vocabulary. The paper therefore prevents merging across character categories (letters, punctuation, etc.), with an exception for spaces. The final vocabulary is 50,257 tokens.

The benefit: the model can be evaluated on any language modeling dataset regardless of preprocessing, tokenization, or vocabulary size. The <UNK> token is extremely rare in WebText, appearing only 26 times in 40 billion bytes.

sections.h: Model: GPT-1's architecture in four sizes

blocks.p: The model mostly follows GPT-1, with a few changes:

list: **Layer normalization is moved to the input of each sub-block** (similar to a pre-activation residual network), with an extra layer normalization after the final self-attention block. This "pre-norm" design later became standard for large models because it makes very deep networks easier to train.

**Residual-layer initialization is scaled down with depth** — initial weights are multiplied by 1/√N, where N is the number of residual layers. More layers mean more accumulation on the residual path, and this scaling keeps the values from growing layer by layer.
**Vocabulary expanded to 50,257**; **context length increased from 512 to 1,024 tokens**; batch size increased to 512.

blocks.p: The paper trains four models with roughly log-uniform sizes. The smallest is equivalent to the original GPT, the second-smallest is equivalent to the largest BERT, and the largest is GPT-2. Each model's learning rate was manually tuned for the best perplexity on a held-out 5% sample of WebText.

fig.title: Four models: the paper's parameter counts don't match the configurations
fig.subtitle: The "estimated from config" column is our calculation: about 12 × d_{model}^{2} per layer, plus 50,257 × d_{model} for token embeddings and 1,024 × d_{model} for position embeddings, ignoring layer normalization and other small terms. Amber indicates GPT-2.
fig.note: All four models are larger by this estimate than the paper reports. The smallest model's 117M is close to the roughly 116M you get from GPT-1's configuration (40,000-token vocabulary, 512 context), which suggests the paper reused GPT-1's number and did not account for the larger vocabulary and longer context. OpenAI later acknowledged in its open-source release notes that the original parameter counts were wrong, revising them to 124M, 355M, 774M, and 1.5B — matching these estimates.

blocks.p: The paper also stresses that **all models still underfit WebText**; with more training, held-out perplexity keeps dropping. In Figure 4, train and test perplexity are nearly identical and fall together as models grow — so even GPT-2 is far from simply memorizing the training data.

quiz.q: Why does GPT-2 use byte-level BPE rather than BPE over Unicode characters?
options: Unicode has too many characters: the base vocabulary would exceed 130,000. Bytes have only 256 values and can represent any string
So the model learns only English
quiz.why: The goal is to let the model compute probabilities for arbitrary text. A byte-level base vocabulary has only 256 entries, so there are no out-of-vocabulary tokens, and merging can then learn common subwords. The paper also adds a rule that keeps dog and its trailing punctuation from merging into many redundant tokens.

sections.h: How to make it do tasks without fine-tuning: write the task as a prompt

blocks.p: All results are zero-shot: no parameters are updated. You carefully arrange the context the model sees, then let it generate or score. Different tasks use different prompt formats:

fig.title: The same language model does different tasks with different contexts
fig.subtitle: Compiled from section 3 of the paper
rows: Greedy decoding; the continuation is the answer
Generate 100 tokens with top-k sampling (k = 2), then take the first 3 sentences
Examples of "English sentence = French sentence" + an English sentence + "="
Greedy decoding; take the first generated sentence
A few QA examples + a new question
Fill the sentence with each candidate word in turn
Compare the probability of each filled sentence and choose the highest

plain.title: Append "TL;DR:" to the article
plain.text: On the web, many long posts end with "TL;DR:" (too long; didn't read) followed by a one-line summary. Feed GPT-2 an article with "TL;DR:" at the end, and its most likely continuation is a summary. No training needed — swap the prompt and you've swapped the task.

callout.title: TL;DR is the web's natural prompt
callout.text: TL;DR stands for Too Long; Didn't Read, and people online often add it at the end of a long post followed by a sentence or two of summary. The model has seen this pattern countless times in WebText, so when it sees "TL;DR:" it knows to write a summary. The paper ran a control: removing the TL;DR prompt lowered the combined summarization score by 6.4 points, showing that natural language alone can evoke a specific behavior. Today's prompt engineering has one of its earliest roots here.

quiz.q: The paper says removing the "TL;DR:" prompt lowers summarization scores by 6.4 points. What does that show?
options: TL;DR is a special control symbol
The model learned from training data that TL;DR is usually followed by a summary, so natural language can specify the task
quiz.why: To the model, TL;DR is just ordinary text with no special design. It learned from the web that "TL;DR is followed by a summary," so a small prompt switches its behavior. That is exactly the evidence that language itself can specify a task.

sections.h: Result 1: language modeling — records on 7 of 8 datasets

blocks.p: First, the model's core job: language modeling. WebText-trained models were evaluated directly on other language modeling benchmarks — no training, no fine-tuning. These datasets contain aggressively standardized text (disconnected punctuation and contractions, shuffled sentences, even <UNK> tokens), so for GPT-2 they are clearly out-of-distribution. The paper uses invertible de-tokenizers to remove these artifacts, which improves GPT-2's perplexity by 2.5 to 5 points.

fig.title: Zero-shot language modeling: GPT-2 beats the prior best on every dataset except 1BW
fig.subtitle: From Table 3 of the paper. PPL is perplexity (lower is better), ACC is accuracy in %, and BPB / BPC are bits per byte / per character (lower is better). Blue indicates GPT-2.
fig.note: The biggest gains came on small datasets like Penn Treebank and WikiText-2, which have only one to two million training tokens. 1BW was the only miss: the paper argues it is the largest and is shuffled at the sentence level, which destroys long-range structure.

blocks.p: **LAMBADA** is designed to test long-range dependencies: the model must predict the final word of a sentence, and a human needs at least the preceding 50 tokens of context to guess it. GPT-2 cuts perplexity from 99.8 to 8.6 and lifts accuracy from 19% to 52.66%. After analyzing errors, the paper finds that most wrong answers are fluent continuations that just cannot serve as the sentence's **final word**; adding a stopword-filtering rule raises accuracy to 63.24%, 4 points above the prior best.
**Winograd commonsense reasoning**: GPT-2 scores 70.70%, 7 points above the prior best. But the paper cautions that this dataset has only 273 questions.

sections.h: Result 2: zero-shot task performance — some close, some far behind

fig.title: Zero-shot results on five tasks: reading comprehension nears supervised models, while summarization and translation remain rudimentary
fig.subtitle: From sections 3.5–3.8 and Table 4 of the paper. Amber highlights reading comprehension, the best result.
rows: Matches or beats 3 of 4 supervised baselines; the best BERT system is close to the human score of 89
Random 3-sentence baseline: 20.98; first-3-sentences baseline: 31.55; prior best: 32.75
Best unsupervised machine translation at the time: 33.5
Slightly worse than word-by-word substitution using a bilingual dictionary
Simple baseline that answers with the most common answer for each question type: 1.0%; retrieve-and-extract systems: 30% to 50%

blocks.p: **Reading comprehension** is closest to usable: given the passage, dialogue history, and a final “A:”, GPT-2 scores 55 F1 with greedy decoding, while the supervised systems it is compared against trained on over 127,000 human-written question-answer pairs. However, the paper finds that it often falls back on simple retrieval heuristics — for example, when asked “who,” it picks a person's name from the passage.

**Summarization** looks like summarization, but it often only summarizes the end of the article or gets details wrong (such as how many cars were in a crash, or whether a logo was on a hat or a shirt). By ROUGE, it is only slightly better than randomly selecting three sentences.

**Translation** was the biggest surprise for the authors: they had deliberately filtered non-English pages out of WebText, and a post-hoc language detector found only about 10 MB of French — roughly 500 times less than the French monolingual corpora typically used in unsupervised translation research. Even so, GPT-2 scored 11.5 BLEU on French-to-English, beating several unsupervised translation baselines. English-to-French scored only 5 BLEU, because the model's French ability is far weaker than its English.

**Question answering** tests how much knowledge is stored in the model's parameters. GPT-2 achieves only 4.1% exact match, but the smallest model does not even beat the 1.0% baseline of answering with the most common answer for each question type, and GPT-2 answers correctly 5.3 times as often as the smallest model. Its confidence is also reasonably reliable: on the 1% of questions it is most confident about, accuracy reaches 63.1%.

fig.note: A footnote adds a small aside: lead author Alec considers himself good at trivia, so he tested himself on 100 random questions under the same setup and got 17 right. He then adds that he actually only got 14 right; the other 3 he “should have gotten,” but the questions leaked the answer.

blocks.p: One pattern holds across all tasks: **performance improves steadily with model size**. Figure 1 of the paper shows zero-shot performance on reading comprehension, translation, summarization, and QA all rising with parameter count; the abstract calls the improvement “log-linear.” This is the phenomenon GPT-3 and the Scaling Laws paper later studied systematically.

With this much training data, could the test questions already have appeared in training? The paper runs a dedicated overlap analysis: it puts every 8-gram (8 consecutive words) from the WebText training set into a Bloom filter, then checks how many 8-grams from each test set also appear in the training data.

fig.title: Most test sets overlap no more with WebText than with their own training sets
fig.subtitle: How many 8-grams in each test set also appear in training data; from Table 6 of the paper. Amber indicates 1BW.
columns: Overlap with its own training set
fig.note: For common language modeling test sets, overlap with WebText ranges from 1% to 6%, averaging 3.2%; overlap with their own training sets averages 5.9%, actually higher. 1BW's overlap with its own training set is close to 13.2%. The paper also finds that one article in WikiText-103's test set is also in its own training set.

plain.title: Learned, or just seen the exact question?
plain.text: If the test questions themselves were already in pages the model read, good scores could simply mean the model memorized the answers. The paper checks how much the test sets duplicate WebText and finds that most overlap no more with WebText than with their own training sets, so the results are not mainly from memorization.

list: **LAMBADA**: average overlap 1.2%. Removing every sample with overlap changes perplexity from 8.6 to 8.7 and accuracy from 63.2% to 62.9% — a small effect.

**CoQA**: about 15% of news articles appear in WebText, and the model scores about 3 points higher F1 on those articles. Overall, overlap adds about 0.5 to 1.0 F1. CoQA was released after WebText's cutoff, so the questions and answers themselves are not in the training data.
**Winograd**: only 10 questions have 8-gram overlap with WebText, and 2 of those are false positives.

blocks.p: The paper concludes that data overlap gives a **small but consistent** advantage, but for most datasets the overlap is no worse than the overlap between their own training and test sets. It recommends that n-gram overlap deduplication become a standard check when building NLP datasets in the future.

list: **The parameter counts are wrong**: the paper's Table 2 figures of 117M, 345M, 762M, and 1542M are all smaller than what the configurations imply (see the estimate table above). The smallest model's 117M is close to the size estimated from GPT-1's configuration, so the larger vocabulary and longer context were likely left out.

**Two ways of stating the data size**: section 2.1 says WebText is 40 GB of text, and section 3.1 says <UNK> appears 26 times in “40 billion bytes.” 40 GB is about 40 billion bytes, so the two statements agree; they are just different units, not two different datasets.

**What “7 out of 8” actually counts**: Table 3 has 10 columns, but LAMBADA's perplexity and accuracy count as one dataset, and CBT's two question types also count as one. That makes 8 datasets, and GPT-2 fails to beat the prior best only on 1BW.

**The paper does not actually describe GPT-2's release details**: when OpenAI released it, concerns about misuse (such as mass-producing fake news) led it to publish only the smallest model at first, release larger versions in stages over several months, and only release the full 1.5-billion-parameter model in November 2019. This staged-release decision was highly controversial at the time, but the paper itself does not discuss it.

blocks.p: The paper's discussion section is measured:

list: **Zero-shot is far from practical**: reading comprehension is competitive, while summarization only “qualitatively resembles” the real thing and is still rudimentary by the metrics. As the paper writes, from a practical standpoint, GPT-2's zero-shot performance is nowhere near usable.

**Many tasks are still at chance level**: the authors acknowledge that on many practical tasks GPT-2 is certainly no better than random guessing; even on QA and translation, it only starts to beat simple baselines once the model is large enough.

**The one-direction limitation**: the paper notes it is unclear whether more data and capacity for GPT-2 can make up for the inefficiency of unidirectional representations that BERT has already demonstrated. They plan to fine-tune GPT-2 on benchmarks such as GLUE to answer this.

blocks.p: **What came next**. The paper's conclusion says that high-capacity models trained on sufficiently large and diverse data begin to learn many tasks without explicit supervision. A year later, GPT-3 (2020) took that claim to its extreme: 175 billion parameters, and instead of zero-shot prompting it used **few-shot prompting** — a few examples in the context — to approach or even beat fine-tuned models on many tasks. The Scaling Laws paper that same year turned “bigger is better” into a predictable power law.

GPT-2 itself left several lasting marks: pre-layer normalization became the standard architecture for large models; byte-level BPE was adopted by many later models; and the idea of evoking a task with a prompt later grew into the entire discipline of prompt engineering.

sections.h: Check yourself: did you get it?

quiz.q: Why does the paper say the global optimum of the supervised objective is also the global optimum of the unsupervised objective?
options: Because they use the same optimizer
Because if the task, input, and answer are all written in the same text, predicting the answer is just part of predicting the next word
Because supervised data is a subset of unsupervised data
Because language models don't need labels
quiz.why: When the answer is also part of the text, the supervised objective is simply “predict the next word at those answer positions,” which is a subset of the language-model objective. The paper also cautions that this only holds in principle; the real question is whether the objective can be optimized well enough in practice, and early experiments show learning is much slower than with direct supervision.

quiz.q: Many of GPT-2's incorrect LAMBADA answers are fluent continuations but not the sentence's final word. How does the paper improve on this?
options: Add a stopword-filtering rule that approximates the constraint that the answer must be the sentence-final word
Only allow words that appear in the context
quiz.why: The paper adds stopword filtering and accuracy rises from 52.66% to 63.24%. The previous best method restricted outputs to words in the context, but the paper finds this actually hurts GPT-2, because 19% of the answers are not in the context.

blocks.p: After reading this, you should be able to answer these questions:

list: What does p(output | input, task) mean? Why does language let us specify tasks?
How was WebText built? Why remove Wikipedia?
What problem does byte-level BPE solve?
What three architectural changes does GPT-2 make to GPT-1?
For zero-shot summarization, translation, and reading comprehension, what does the model see in each case?
Which tasks are close to usable, and which are still poor?
How does the paper check for overlap between test data and training data? What does it conclude?
Why don't the paper's reported parameter counts match the counts computed from the configurations?
